Project Summary:  
730 Stanyan Street (the “Project”) will be a new mixed-use building located in the Haight- 
Ashbury neighborhood directly across the street from Golden Gate Park. Located on a 
parcel directly purchased by the City and subject to a ground lease, the Project will feature 
new affordable housing with 160 residential rental units ranging in income restrictions from 
0% to 80% MOHCD AMI for families and Transitional Age Youth (TAY), including those who 
were formerly homeless. The project will include one manager’s unit and comprise a mix of 
studios, 1-, 2- and 3-bedroom units. The project will include 40 Local Operating Subsidy 
Program (LOSP) units (split between TAY and family households) and, in addition to 
community spaces for residents, there will be five separate commercial spaces on the 
ground floor to serve the residents and the community.  
 
Each of these five spaces will be operated by various non-profit partners to provide early 
childhood education (child care center), transitional age youth services/drop-in center, tech 
training, a senior center, and, potentially, a low-cost restaurant or cafe. 
 
This request is intended to provide a commitment of MOHCD gap loan funding, in 
connection with applications to California Department of Housing and Community 
Development (HCD) for loans and grants associated with a Summer 2022 HCD Super 
NOFA. This request is also in support of August 2022 applications, with CDLAC, for 4% tax 
credits and tax-exempt bonds (limited partner equity). The Project will return to Loan 
Committee for its final gap commitment once it has obtained financing commitments from 
the State. 
 
The Project is aiming for a minimum of LEED Gold and Passive House certifications for 
green standards. In addition to public art at multiple exterior locations, the project will be the 
first to meet City Planning’s AB 168 agreement process to pay tribute to Native American 
land that the Project will be built on. Additionally, the Project is developing an affordable 
marketing plan to proactively reach out to underserved BIPOC populations, including seniors 
in District 5.

PRINCIPAL DEVELOPMENT ISSUES  
● Unit count and building height. The Request for Qualifications (RFQ) for Developers 
issued by MOHCD described a desired project with 120 units in a six-story building in an 
effort to ensure that the building could be built at a reasonable cost and within MOHCD’s 
funding constraints. However, about one year after the start of the project, MOHCD has 
redirected the Developers to maximize the housing allowed under the Zoning, which has 
led to redesign of the project to an 8-story building with 160 units. See Section 4.2 for 
further information. 
 
● LOSP Subsidy. The proposed resident mix includes 20 LOSP subsidized units for 
families and 20 LOSP subsidized units (studios and one-bedroom units) for TAY 
households. In addition, there are 10 additional units intended for TAY households at 50% 
MOHCD AMI, without a specific subsidy (e.g., LOSP, Continuum of Care, or other 
programs). The projected rents for these 10 TAY units are $1,213, for eight studios, and 
$1,386 for two one-bedroom units. Pending further discussion with the City’s Department 
of Homelessness and Supportive Housing (HSH), the Sponsor may consider increasing 
the LOSP subsidy to include these 10 units. See Section 7.7 for further information. 
 
● Community outreach. The Haight-Ashbury neighborhood includes a wide array of active 
community groups with a history of very close involvement with this site. Many of these 
groups have differing views about the best development plan for the site. There has been 
a recent focus on feedback from stakeholders who want to add units with preference for 
seniors. Please see Section 3.1 for further explanation. 
 
● Cost Containment. The re-design from 6 stories to 8 stories has extended the overall 
project timeline. In addition, having three street frontages with neighborhood facing wall 
treatments, curved wall elements, related street and sidewalk improvements, and Type 
I construction (concrete), make this Project more expensive than other projects in 
MOHCD's pipeline. Market and supply chain challenges have also resulted in 
construction estimates that are ten to fifteen percent higher than initially forecast. 
Please see Section 4.4 for further explanation and recommended conditions of loan 
approval. 
 
● Commercial Space. The proposed commercial space totals 11,145 sf, and is a 
substantial portion of the ground floor area. The Project includes the cost of developing 
these spaces to the City’s “warm shell” standards. Four of the five commercial spaces are 
anticipated to be community serving and are not revenue generating. The cost of further 
tenant improvements will need to be borne by others besides MOHCD. The COVID-19 
pandemic has created a more uncertain climate for leasing of spaces such as cafes. 
Despite community interest in senior services in this location, no provider has come 
forward during the pandemic in response to an RFP. The Sponsor may need to re-issue 
an RFP in 2023, and/or the Sponsor and the City may consider other uses such as, but 
not limited to, an expanded early childhood education center, assuming interest by a 
provider such as Felton Institute which has been selected for the designated early child 
care center space. Please see Section 3.1.

BACKGROUND 
1.1. 
Project History Leading to This Request.   
Located on Stanyan Street between Haight and Waller Street, 730 Stanyan Street (“Project 
Site”) is the site of a former McDonald’s that occupied the site since the 1960s. During the 
past decade, the McDonald’s developed a reputation as a neighborhood nuisance, leading 
neighbors to complain to the City about problems with crime and drug sales outside of the 
restaurant. These issues became severe enough for the City Attorney to threaten the fast-food 
corporation and franchise operators with legal action. Despite the corporation’s additional 
security measures, the site continued to be the source of neighborhood complaints. In 2018, 
the City entered into a Purchase and Sale Agreement with McDonald’s with the plan of 
constructing 100% affordable housing. As required by the Purchase and Sale Agreement, the 
City coordinated building demolition. In response to the COVID-19 health crisis, the City’s 
Department of Emergency Management opted to use the site as a safe sleeping village. The 
Site is now vacant and fenced off. The proposed building operating budget includes 24-hour 
front desk staffing, two dedicated janitors, and two maintenance staff.  
Some community members have requested that the Project include a set aside of senior units. 
However, the Project will not be able to designate senior units due to federal fair housing laws 
that make intergenerational housing infeasible at this site.

income residents in Chinatown. Understanding all organizations have room to grow in addressing 
institutionalized racism, Chinatown CDC has approached this with intention, by modifying

communities they serve, providing opportunities for BIPOC residents to engage with the 
neighborhood planning process, and working to heal historic divides between Asian Americans and 
other BIPOC and White communities.

housing, social and economic mobility, education, health, and housing assistance to support 
intergenerational wealth building in BIPOC communities. Chinatown CDC uses a Community 
Building and Engagement (CB&E) model of resident service provision, which posits that being 
socially connected and active in one’s community not only enhances one’s quality of life but is a

The CB&E model prioritizes residents’ experiences, ideas, and skills in the creation of programming.

embrace Golden Gate Park across Stanyan Street. A second major “scoop” or curved façade 
occurs at the corner of Stanyan and Haight Streets above the 40-ft datum. At both scoops, the 
volume of the building is pushed away from Stanyan Street to create a dynamically shaped 
volume of ins and outs to establish multiple corners for optimized corner views towards the Park 
and access (to daylight. A small “scoop” occurs on Waller Street where the proposed building 
gently meets the existing adjacent residential building set back from the property line. The bulk of 
the exposed surfaces will be clad in GFRC (glass-fiber reinforced concrete), which is light-weight, 
resilient and repeatable prefabricated material with small, medium and large “waves” molded in, 
reflective of the undulating rhythm of Victorian facades in the neighborhood. The ground floor 
facade will be built with prefabricated concrete and storefronts for combination of durability and 
visibility, respectively.

5th floor terrace will provide urban agriculture for vegetable production managed by a professional 
group. The building is employing Passive House standards for efficient exterior construction 
requiring a high level of air tightness and continual filtered fresh air circulation with individual ERV 
(Energy Recovery Ventilators) for units for energy savings and resident comfort. The all-electric 
building will have photovoltaic panels to offset energy consumption.

         7.7  Local Operating Subsidy Program (LOSP) & No Place Like Home (NPLH) Units 
The property will feature 40 apartments with operating funds provided under a separate Local 
Operating Subsidy Program (LOSP) contract administered by MOHCD and HSH, to provide 
ongoing supportive housing services. Through 15-year grant agreements with MOHCD and HSH, 
which are subject to annual appropriations by the City’s Board of Supervisors, LOSP pays the 
difference between the cost of operating housing for persons experiencing homelessness and all 
other sources of operating revenue for a given project, such as tenant rental payments and other 
operating subsidies. 
Capital costs for 20 of the 40 proposed LOSP Subsidy units will also be funded through the State’s 
No Place Like Home (NPLH) program. The NPLH program dedicates up to $2 billion in State bond 
proceeds, across California, for the development of permanent supportive housing, for persons 
who are in need of mental health services and are experiencing homelessness, chronic 
homelessness, or who are at risk of chronic homelessness.
